title: Python
sources: Python Automation Engineer Handbook (complete edition, Oct 2026)

challenges.title: Hashable inventory keys
challenges.description: Dictionary keys must be hashable. Pick the value that can key a rack-inventory dict.
challenges.instructions: Which of these values can be used as a dictionary key?
hints: Only immutable built-in containers are hashable.
Lists, dicts and sets are all mutable.
challenges.explanation:
A tuple of hashable elements is itself hashable, so ('rack12', 7) works as a key.
       Lists, dicts and sets are mutable and therefore unhashable; using one raises TypeError: unhashable type.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 7 Data Structures; Ch. 39 B2

challenges.title: Equal is not identical
challenges.description: Compare two firmware-version lists with == and is.
challenges.instructions: Type exactly what this program prints. Each print() call is one line.
hints: == compares values; is compares object identity.
Two list literals always create two objects.
challenges.explanation:
== calls __eq__ and compares contents, so the lists are equal. is checks whether both names refer to
            the same object; each list literal creates a new object, so the identity check is False.
            Use is only for singletons such as None.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 3 Operators; Ch. 39 B3
challenges.code:
expected = ["2.14", "1.9"]
actual = ["2.14", "1.9"]
print(expected == actual, expected is actual)

verify.template:
expected = ["2.14", "1.9"]
actual = ["2.14", "1.9"]
print(expected == actual, expected is actual)

challenges.title: append vs extend
challenges.description: Build an ipmitool command line and count its parts.
challenges.instructions: Type exactly what this program prints. Each print() call is one line.
hints: append adds exactly one element, whatever it is.
What is that one element here?
challenges.explanation:
append adds its argument as a single element, so the inner list becomes the 4th item.
            extend(["sdr", "list"]) would have added two separate strings and produced length 5.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 7 Data Structures; Ch. 39 B5
challenges.code:
cmd = ["ipmitool", "-I", "lanplus"]
cmd.append(["sdr", "list"])
print(len(cmd), cmd[-1])

verify.template:
cmd = ["ipmitool", "-I", "lanplus"]
cmd.append(["sdr", "list"])
print(len(cmd), cmd[-1])

challenges.title: Format a temperature
challenges.description: Print a CPU temperature rounded to one decimal place with an f-string.
challenges.instructions: Fill the blank so the program prints: CPU0: 41.3 C
hints: Format specifiers go after a colon inside the braces.
f means fixed-point; the number before it is the precision.
challenges.explanation:
The format spec :.1f renders a float in fixed-point notation with one digit after the decimal point,
         rounding 41.256 to 41.3.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 4 Input, Output and String Formatting
challenges.code:
temp = 41.256
print(f"CPU0: {temp____} C")

verify.template:
temp = 41.256
print(f"CPU0: {temp{{answer}}} C")

challenges.title: A reading of zero is valid
challenges.description: A sensor function returns None when no reading is available and a float otherwise; 0.0 is a valid reading.
challenges.instructions: Which condition correctly detects a missing reading?
hints: 0.0 is falsy.
Check for the specific sentinel value.
challenges.explanation:
reading is None is true only for the missing case. if not reading would also fire for a valid 0.0 reading,
       because 0.0 is falsy. Comparing with False is wrong for the same reason (0.0 == False is True).
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 5 Conditional Statements; Ch. 39 B11, B14

challenges.title: Slicing a serial number
challenges.description: Extract the year and the suffix from a board serial number.
challenges.instructions: Type exactly what this program prints. Each print() call is one line.
hints: Indexes start at 0 and the stop index is excluded.
Negative indexes count from the end.
challenges.explanation:
serial[3:7] takes characters 3, 4, 5 and 6, which are "2026". serial[-4:] takes the last four
            characters, "AX91".
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 2 Variables, Data Types and Memory; Ch. 39 B16
challenges.code:
serial = "SN-2026-AX91"
print(serial[3:7], serial[-4:])

verify.template:
serial = "SN-2026-AX91"
print(serial[3:7], serial[-4:])

challenges.title: Deduplicate, keep order
challenges.description: A scan returns host names with duplicates. Remove the duplicates but keep first-seen order.
challenges.instructions: Write one expression that evaluates to the deduplicated list, in first-seen order. Use the variable hosts and the dict.fromkeys idiom.
hints: Dictionaries preserve insertion order.
dict.fromkeys(iterable) creates one key per unique item.
challenges.explanation:
dict.fromkeys(hosts) keeps the first occurrence of every key in insertion order (guaranteed since
           Python 3.7); wrapping it in list() gives the ordered unique hosts. list(set(hosts)) also removes
           duplicates but loses the order.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 7 Data Structures; Ch. 39 B15
challenges.code:
hosts = ["u07", "u03", "u07", "u12", "u03"]
# your expression:

challenges.title: The disappearing host list
challenges.description: This loop crashes with TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not iterable.
challenges.instructions: What is the bug?
hints: What does list.sort() return?
Compare sort() with sorted().
challenges.explanation:
list.sort() sorts the list in place and returns None. Assigning that result back to hosts throws the list
        away. Either call hosts.sort() on its own line or write hosts = sorted(hosts).
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 7 Data Structures; Ch. 39 B17
challenges.code:
hosts = ["u12", "u03", "u07"]
hosts = hosts.sort()
for host in hosts:
    print("checking", host)
options: Strings cannot be sorted, so sort() fails
list.sort() sorts in place and returns None, so hosts becomes None
The for loop must use range(len(hosts))

challenges.title: Dictionary lookup cost
challenges.description: Redfish responses become dicts, and automation code looks keys up constantly.
challenges.instructions: What is the average time complexity of looking up a key in a Python dict?
hints: A dict is a hash table.
The key's hash points straight to its slot.
challenges.explanation:
A dict is a hash table: the key's hash locates its slot directly, so lookup, insertion and deletion
       are O(1) on average. Worst-case collisions are possible but rare with good hashes.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 7 Data Structures; Ch. 39 B4

challenges.title: get() with defaults
challenges.description: Read fan speeds where some fans are missing and some report no value.
challenges.instructions: Type exactly what this program prints. Each print() call is one line.
hints: The default is used only when the key is absent.
Is fan2 absent?
challenges.explanation:
get() returns the default only when the key is missing. fan3 is missing, so 0 is returned. fan2
            exists with the value None, so None is returned, not the default.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 7 Data Structures
challenges.code:
fans = {"fan1": 4200, "fan2": None}
print(fans.get("fan3", 0), fans.get("fan2", 0))

verify.template:
fans = {"fan1": 4200, "fan2": None}
print(fans.get("fan3", 0), fans.get("fan2", 0))

challenges.title: The shared default list
challenges.description: A helper records test results in a history list.
challenges.instructions: Type exactly what this program prints. Each print() call is one line.
hints: Default values are evaluated once, when def runs.
Both calls see the same list object.
challenges.explanation:
The default list is created once at function definition time and reused by every call that omits
            history, so results accumulate. Use history=None and create a new list inside the function.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 8 Functions; Ch. 39 I4
challenges.code:
def record(result, history=[]):
    history.append(result)
    return history

record("pass")
print(record("fail"))

verify.template:
def record(result, history=[]):
    history.append(result)
    return history

record("pass")
print(record("fail"))

challenges.title: Filter hot sensors
challenges.description: Keep only the sensors hotter than 80 °C with a dict comprehension.
challenges.instructions: Fill the blank so the comprehension iterates over key–value pairs.
hints: You need both the key and the value in each iteration.
keys() and values() give only half.
challenges.explanation:
dict.items() yields (key, value) pairs that unpack into name and t. The comprehension keeps the
         pairs where t > 80.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 9 Comprehensions and Iteration

challenges.title: Missing devices
challenges.description: Compare the expected inventory with what the scan found.
challenges.instructions: Write one expression that returns the devices in expected but not in found, as a sorted list. Both are sets; use the - operator.
hints: Set difference keeps items of the left set that are not in the right set.
sorted() turns any iterable into a sorted list.
challenges.explanation:
expected - found is the set difference: devices that were expected but not discovered. sorted() makes
           the result deterministic, which matters for readable test reports.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 7 Data Structures (sets for comparing inventories)

testCases.input: expected = {nvme0, nvme1, nic0, psu1}; found = {nvme0, psu1}

challenges.title: *args and **kwargs
challenges.description: A command wrapper forwards extra arguments.
challenges.instructions: Type exactly what this program prints. Each print() call is one line.
hints: *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple.
sorted() on a dict sorts its keys.
challenges.explanation:
cmd receives "ipmitool"; the two extra positional strings go into args; the keyword arguments go into
            kwargs. sorted(kwargs) iterates over the dict's keys and returns them alphabetically.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 8 Functions; Ch. 39 B7

challenges.title: Can a tuple change?
challenges.description: Consider t = ([], 5).
challenges.instructions: Which statement is true?
hints: Immutability applies to the tuple's own slots.
The slot holds a reference to a list.
challenges.explanation:
The tuple's slots cannot be reassigned, but slot 0 refers to a mutable list, which can still be changed.
       Because it contains a list, t is also unhashable and cannot be a dict key.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 39 B2
options: t can be used as a dictionary key
t[0].append(1) raises TypeError because tuples are immutable
t[0].append(1) works and changes what t displays
t[1] = 6 works because 5 is an int

challenges.title: Stable sorting
challenges.description: Order components by priority; two share the same priority.
challenges.instructions: Type exactly what this program prints. Each print() call is one line.
hints: Python's sort is stable.
Items with equal keys keep their original relative order.
challenges.explanation:
sorted() orders by the second element. fan and cpu both have key 3; because the sort is stable they
            stay in their original order, fan before cpu.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 39 B17 (stable sorts)
challenges.code:
results = [("fan", 3), ("psu", 1), ("cpu", 3), ("nic", 2)]
print([name for name, _ in sorted(results, key=lambda r: r[1])])

verify.template:
results = [("fan", 3), ("psu", 1), ("cpu", 3), ("nic", 2)]
print([name for name, _ in sorted(results, key=lambda r: r[1])])

challenges.title: Zeros that will not go away
challenges.description: This code is meant to remove all zero readings, but prints [12, 0, 7].
challenges.instructions: What causes the wrong result?
hints: Track the loop's index as items shift left.
After a removal, the next element moves into the current position.
challenges.explanation:
The loop advances by index. Removing the first 0 shifts the second 0 into the current index, and the loop
        then moves past it. Build a new list instead: readings = [r for r in readings if r != 0].
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 6 Loops; Ch. 36 Debugging Python Programs
options: remove() deletes every matching value, not just one
print() is called inside the loop
Removing items from a list while iterating over it makes the loop skip elements

challenges.title: Always pass an encoding
challenges.description: with open(path) as f: works on your laptop but fails on a Windows CI agent with UnicodeDecodeError.
challenges.instructions: What is the most reliable fix?
hints: Without encoding=, Python uses the machine's locale default.
Different machines, different defaults.
challenges.explanation:
Without an explicit encoding, open() uses the platform's locale encoding, which differs between machines.
       Passing encoding="utf-8" makes the behaviour the same everywhere.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 12 File Handling; Ch. 39 B10; Ch. 38 Troubleshooting
options: Open the file in binary mode and ignore the content
Wrap the read in a bare except

challenges.title: Split with a limit
challenges.description: Split a log line into date, time, level and message, keeping colons in the message.
challenges.instructions: Type exactly what this program prints. Each print() call is one line.
hints: The second argument to split() is the maximum number of splits.
After 3 splits the rest stays together.
challenges.explanation:
split(" ", 3) splits at most three times, giving exactly four fields. Everything after the third space,
            including further spaces, stays in msg.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Project P3 Log Parser and Error-Summary Generator
challenges.code:
line = "2026-10-21 14:02:11 ERROR psu2: input lost: AC"
date, time, level, msg = line.split(" ", 3)
print(level, "|", msg)

verify.template:
line = "2026-10-21 14:02:11 ERROR psu2: input lost: AC"
date, time, level, msg = line.split(" ", 3)
print(level, "|", msg)

challenges.title: Capture the fan speed
challenges.description: Pull the numeric speed out of a fan log line with a regular expression.
challenges.instructions: Fill the blank so the program prints 4200.
hints: A match object exposes captured groups.
Group 1 is the first pair of parentheses.
challenges.explanation:
m.group(1) returns the text captured by the first parenthesised group, "4200"; int() converts it.
         Check that m is not None before using it in real parsers.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 17 Regular Expressions
challenges.code:
import re
line = "fan3 speed=4200 rpm"
m = re.search(r"speed=(\d+)", line)
print(int(m.____(1)))

verify.template:
import re
line = "fan3 speed=4200 rpm"
m = re.search(r"speed=(\d+)", line)
print(int(m.{{answer}}(1)))

challenges.title: Most common log levels
challenges.description: Summarise log levels for an error report.
challenges.instructions: Type exactly what this program prints. Each print() call is one line.
hints: most_common(n) returns (item, count) tuples.
Count each level.
challenges.explanation:
Counter counts each level: ERROR 3, INFO 2, WARN 1. most_common(2) returns the two most frequent as a
            list of (item, count) tuples.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 18 Standard Library Mastery; Project P3
challenges.code:
from collections import Counter
levels = ["INFO", "ERROR", "WARN", "ERROR", "INFO", "ERROR"]
print(Counter(levels).most_common(2))

verify.template:
from collections import Counter
levels = ["INFO", "ERROR", "WARN", "ERROR", "INFO", "ERROR"]
print(Counter(levels).most_common(2))

challenges.title: Collect error lines
challenges.description: Keep only the lines containing ERROR, without surrounding whitespace.
challenges.instructions: Write a list comprehension over lines that keeps lines containing "ERROR" and strips each one. Use line as the loop variable.
hints: The filter goes after the for clause.
strip() removes leading and trailing whitespace, including newlines.
challenges.explanation:
The comprehension filters with if "ERROR" in line and transforms each kept line with strip(), which
           removes the newline and any leading spaces.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 9 Comprehensions; Project P3
challenges.code:
lines = ["boot ok
", "ERROR fan1 stalled
", "  ERROR psu2 lost
"]
# your expression:

testCases.input:
lines = ["boot ok
", "ERROR fan1 stalled
", "  ERROR psu2 lost
"]

acceptedAnswers: [line.strip() for line in lines if "ERROR" in line]
[line.strip() for line in lines if "ERROR" in line.strip()]

lines = ["boot ok
", "ERROR fan1 stalled
", "  ERROR psu2 lost
"]
print({{answer}})

challenges.title: Find completion codes
challenges.description: Extract two-digit hex completion codes from an IPMI trace.
challenges.instructions: Type exactly what this program prints. Each print() call is one line.
hints: {2} means exactly two hex digits.
\b requires a word boundary after the digits.
challenges.explanation:
findall returns every non-overlapping match. 0x1 has only one hex digit, so it does not match
            0x[0-9A-Fa-f]{2}.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 17 Regular Expressions
challenges.code:
import re
trace = "cc=0xD5 retry cc=0x00 len=0x1"
print(re.findall(r"\b0x[0-9A-Fa-f]{2}\b", trace))

verify.template:
import re
trace = "cc=0xD5 retry cc=0x00 len=0x1"
print(re.findall(r"\b0x[0-9A-Fa-f]{2}\b", trace))

challenges.title: load vs loads
challenges.description: You have a Redfish response body as a str in memory.
challenges.instructions: Which call parses it into Python objects?
hints: The trailing s stands for string.
load() expects a file object.
challenges.explanation:
json.loads parses a str; json.load reads from a file-like object. dumps/dump go the other way,
       serialising Python objects to JSON.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 13 Working with Structured Data

challenges.title: One pass only
challenges.description: A generator yields the line numbers of errors.
challenges.instructions: Type exactly what this program prints. Each print() call is one line.
hints: enumerate(lines, 1) starts counting at 1.
What is left in a generator after it has been consumed?
challenges.explanation:
The first list() consumes the generator and gets [2, 4]. A generator can be iterated only once, so the
            second list() gets nothing.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 15 Iterators, Generators; Ch. 39 I1

challenges.title: One test too many
challenges.description: results.csv has a header row and 40 result rows, but the script reports 41 tests executed.
challenges.instructions: What is the bug?
hints: What is the first row of the file?
csv.reader does not know which row is the header.
challenges.explanation:
csv.reader returns every row, including the header. csv.DictReader consumes the header as field names,
        or you can call next(reader) before counting. newline="" is the recommended way to open CSV files.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 13 Working with Structured Data; Project P4
challenges.code:
import csv
with open("results.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    rows = list(csv.reader(f))
print(f"{len(rows)} tests executed")
options: newline="" adds an extra empty row
The header row is counted as a test; use csv.DictReader or skip the first row
The file must be opened in binary mode for csv

challenges.title: Running commands safely
challenges.description: A health check pings a host name read from a configuration file.
challenges.instructions: Which call is the safest?
hints: Think about a host value like 'x; rm -rf ~'.
Which option also stops a hung command?
challenges.explanation:
Passing an argument list without shell=True means the host is never interpreted by a shell, so it cannot
       inject commands. capture_output and text collect output as str, and timeout prevents a hung ping from
       blocking the run.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 28 Linux and Command-Line Automation; Ch. 34 Security and Reliability

challenges.title: finally always runs
challenges.description: A check function returns while a cleanup block is pending.
challenges.instructions: Type exactly what this program prints. Each print() call is one line.
hints: finally runs before the function actually returns.
The caller prints the return value last.
challenges.explanation:
The return value is computed, then the finally block runs, then the function returns to the caller,
            which prints "ok". This is why cleanup such as closing a BMC session belongs in finally.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 11 Exception Handling; Ch. 39 B6
challenges.code:
def check():
    try:
        print("try")
        return "ok"
    finally:
        print("cleanup")

print(check())

verify.template:
def check():
    try:
        print("try")
        return "ok"
    finally:
        print("cleanup")

print(check())

challenges.title: A clock for timeouts
challenges.description: A wait loop must not break if NTP adjusts the system clock during the test.
challenges.instructions: Fill the blank with the time function suited to measuring timeouts.
hints: Wall-clock time can jump backwards or forwards.
The answer appears later in the same snippet.
challenges.explanation:
time.monotonic() never goes backwards and is unaffected by clock changes, so durations measured with
         it are reliable. time.time() follows the wall clock, which NTP or a user can change mid-test.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 18 Standard Library Mastery; API & Protocol Automation Handbook Q24

challenges.title: Custom exception hierarchy
challenges.description: A lab framework defines its own exceptions.
challenges.instructions: Type exactly what this program prints. Each print() call is one line.
hints: An except clause also catches subclasses.
type(e) is the class that was actually raised.
challenges.explanation:
except LabError catches any subclass, including DeviceTimeout. The object keeps its real class, and
            str(e) is the message passed to the constructor.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 11 Exception Handling; Ch. 14 OOP

challenges.title: All sensors in range
challenges.description: A thermal check passes only if every reading is between 0 and 85 °C inclusive.
challenges.instructions: Write one expression that is True when every value in the dict readings is within 0..85. Use all() with a generator expression and the loop variable v.
hints: Chained comparisons like 0 <= v <= 85 work in Python.
Iterate over readings.values().
challenges.explanation:
all() returns True only if every item of the generator is truthy, and stops at the first False.
           The chained comparison 0 <= v <= 85 checks both bounds at once.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 9 Comprehensions; Project P10 Device-Health Validation
challenges.code:
readings = {"cpu0": 71, "cpu1": 88}
# your expression:
acceptedAnswers: all(0 <= v <= 85 for v in readings.values())
all(v >= 0 and v <= 85 for v in readings.values())

challenges.title: Logging the right way
challenges.description: A test helper logs every BMC request at DEBUG level, but DEBUG is normally switched off.
challenges.instructions: Which call avoids formatting the message when DEBUG is disabled?
hints: When is an f-string evaluated?
logging can defer the % formatting.
challenges.explanation:
With %-style arguments, logging formats the message only if the record is actually emitted. An f-string
       or concatenation is built before the call, even when the level is disabled. print bypasses logging
       configuration entirely.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 30 Logging, Reporting and Observability; Ch. 39 B13

challenges.title: A session context manager
challenges.description: A generator-based context manager wraps a BMC session.
challenges.instructions: Type exactly what this program prints. Each print() call is one line.
hints: Code before yield is setup; the yielded value is bound by as.
finally runs when the with block exits.
challenges.explanation:
Entering the with block runs the code up to yield; the yielded value becomes s. When the block ends,
            execution resumes after yield, and the finally clause prints the close message.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 15 Context Managers; Ch. 39 I3
acceptedAnswers:
open bmc1
using BMC1
close bmc1

verify.expectedOutput:
open bmc1
using BMC1
close bmc1

challenges.title: The always-healthy sensor
challenges.description: A dashboard shows 0.0 °C for a sensor that is actually disconnected.
challenges.instructions: What is the bug?
hints: What happens to the real error?
Is 0.0 distinguishable from a real reading?
challenges.explanation:
A bare except catches everything, even KeyboardInterrupt, and hides the real failure behind a valid-looking
        number. Catch the specific exception you expect and either re-raise it or return None so the caller can
        tell a missing reading from 0.0.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 11 Exception Handling; Ch. 34 Security and Reliability
options: return cannot be used inside try
The bare except swallows every error and returns a plausible-looking value
The function should use a while loop

challenges.title: Run a command and check it
challenges.description: Assemble a small script that runs uptime safely and fails loudly on errors.
challenges.instructions: Put the lines in an order that runs correctly. Indentation is shown.
hints: Imports come first.
Check the return code before trusting stdout.
challenges.explanation:
The module is imported, the command runs with a timeout, a non-zero return code raises with the
            captured stderr, and only then is the output used.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 28 Linux and Command-Line Automation; Project P8
